messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ines, a 61-year-old bus driver with thirty years of impeccable service, arrived at her first session accompanied by her husband, though he waited in the reception area. She described her life as having split into two distinct periods: before the accident, and after. The accident itself happened four months ago, on a bright Tuesday morning. A small sedan, two cars ahead of her bus, swerved to avoid a piece of debris and lost control, spinning directly into the path of an oncoming truck. Ines had slammed on the brakes, the bus lurching to a halt just feet from the collision. She was trapped in her elevated driver’s seat, a helpless observer to the screech of tires, the crush of metal, and then a profound, ringing silence. She saw blood on the shattered windshield of the car, a sight that is now seared into her mind.

In the weeks that followed, the event refused to remain in the past. The memory would ambush her without warning, and when it came, it was not a recollection but a full-sensory reliving. She would be standing in her kitchen and suddenly smell the acrid smoke from the sedan’s engine and feel the phantom vibration of her own bus’s brakes locking up. The memory felt so intensely present that she would sometimes reach out to brace herself against a non-existent dashboard. This vivid re-experiencing relentlessly fed her belief that she had failed in some fundamental way. Each time the scene played out in her mind, she was struck by her own immobility, her inability to have done anything more than watch. The thought became a conviction: she should have been able to protect them, and her failure was unforgivable.

This crushing sense of guilt began to shape her daily existence. The more she dwelled on her perceived inaction, the more frequently the memories would surface, as if her mind were forcing her to re-examine the scene for further proof of her culpability. This constant self-blame also made her hyper-aware of potential dangers on the road. Driving her route, once a source of quiet pride, became an exercise in dread. Any car that braked suddenly or the distant wail of a siren would trigger a jolt of panic. These moments didn't just frighten her; they immediately confirmed her deepest fears about herself. A minor fender-bender on the opposite side of the highway became a personal indictment: 'See? It can happen anywhere, and I am powerless to stop it.' The sight of crumpled metal, no matter how insignificant, was a direct reminder of her failure.

To manage the overwhelming guilt and the terrifyingly real memories, Ines developed a set of rigid, private behaviours. Before starting her bus each morning, she now performs a silent ritual, reciting the names of her children and grandchildren seven times to ensure their safety. She believes this frantic mental act is the only thing preventing another tragedy. The horror of the memory also led her to withdraw from all physical contact. The simple act of her husband placing a hand on her shoulder feels like an unbearable intrusion, a sensory overload that threatens to pull her back to the accident scene. This avoidance has carved a painful distance between them, deepening her sense that her life is no longer worth living.

These strategies have only tightened the trap. The mental rituals, designed to provide control, serve as a constant reminder of the very event she is trying to escape, ensuring the memory remains fresh and accessible. Her avoidance of touch has left her profoundly isolated, reinforcing her belief that she is broken beyond repair. This isolation, in turn, makes it harder to dismiss the intrusive thoughts of her failure. At times, the raw emotion of the trauma—a wave of pure, image-less dread and grief—will wash over her, a feeling she has come to associate with her own worthlessness.

She has come to therapy because the rituals are no longer enough to keep the terror at bay, and the chasm between her and her husband has grown too wide to ignore. She feels exhausted by the constant vigilance, by the mental loops of guilt and fear. Her greatest fear, she stated quietly, is not that another accident will happen, but that she is right about herself—that she is a person who failed when it mattered most, and that she will never be able to forgive herself.

violation_explanations: The causal relationship is absent because the vignette does not describe how the trauma memory makes Ines more hyper-aware of or sensitive to triggering stimuli.
The causal relationship is absent because the vignette does not describe how Ines's safety behaviours (rituals, avoidance) make her more sensitive or hypervigilant to external triggers.
